notes: Ruling slot 23 = Shah dynasty (King Mahendra, partyless Panchayat). Slot 13 = Rastriya Panchayat under PM Kirti Nidhi Bista. Nepali Congress kept in MD slot 3; Nepal Praja Parishad (Tanka Prasad Acharya) in 18. Pro-Moscow, palace-friendly CPN (Rayamajhi) in 4, CPN (Pushpa Lal) in 19, Naxalite Jhapa group in 5. Back to the Village National Campaign in 7; pro-China anti-Indian Panchas in 6. Panchayat class organisations used for 14 (peasants) and 20 (ex-servicemen). No MD sprites listed, so all icons null.

0.name: Rāna Khāndān
0.text:
The Ranas ruled Nepal as hereditary prime ministers from 1846 until the revolution of 1951 and remain the country's richest and most powerful aristocracy. Intermarried with the royal house, they hold senior commands in the army and large estates in the Terai, and Crown Prince Birendra is to marry Aishwarya Rana.

The clan's conservative core favours firm royal authority, military discipline and close ties with Britain, whose Gurkha regiments their forefathers supplied, and with the United States. It fears land reform, the Congress democrats and the communists alike. Its leverage lies in wealth, marriage alliances, the officer corps and the habits of command it never lost.

1.name: Sudhārvādi Panch
1.text:
Within the partyless system a pragmatic wing of Panchas wants the Panchayat order to work better rather than harder. Its best-known figure is Surya Bahadur Thapa, twice prime minister in the 1960s, who drew on Indian and American aid and favoured administrative and economic reform. Around him stand former party politicians, lawyers and senior officials who made their peace with the king after 1960.

They defend the monarchy and the partyless constitution, but want more direct elections, a freer press, decentralised development and good relations with India and the West. They oppose the return of parties. Their leverage lies in administrative experience, donor contacts and a following in the Rastriya Panchayat.

2.name: Snātak Panch
2.text:
The Rastriya Panchayat reserves seats for members elected by university graduates, the one corner of the partyless system where educated opinion can be heard. Liberal critics such as Rishikesh Shaha, a former minister and ambassador to Washington, use it to question royal decrees, corruption and the absence of civil liberties, joined by Kathmandu's lawyers, journalists and teachers.

They ask for the rule of law, an independent judiciary, freedom of the press and association, and a government responsible to the legislature, without necessarily restoring the old parties. Western-educated and open to the West, they are tolerated as a safety valve. Their leverage lies in the capital's educated public and in foreign attention.

3.name: Nepāli Kāngres
3.text:
The Nepali Congress led the 1951 revolution against the Ranas and won two-thirds of the seats in the 1959 elections, only for King Mahendra to dismiss and imprison Prime Minister B. P. Koirala in December 1960 and ban all parties. Koirala was released in October 1968 and now lives in exile in India, with veterans such as Ganesh Man Singh and Krishna Prasad Bhattarai.

The party stands for democratic socialism, a constitutional monarchy with a restored parliament, fundamental rights, land reform and planned development. It is close to the Indian socialists and debates whether to return to armed resistance. Its leverage lies in the Terai, among Biratnagar's workers and with the educated youth.

4.name: Nepāl Kamyunist Pārti (Rāyamājhi)
4.text:
The Communist Party of Nepal, founded in Calcutta in 1949, was banned with all parties after 1960 and has since splintered. Its official wing under the general secretary Keshar Jung Rayamajhi welcomed King Mahendra's takeover as a blow against Indian-backed reaction and seeks to work legally within the Panchayat system, earning the scorn of more radical comrades.

It follows the Soviet line of peaceful transition: land reform, nationalisation of foreign trade, a strong public sector and an anti-imperialist foreign policy close to Moscow. It distrusts the Nepali Congress and Peking alike. Its leverage lies in Soviet patronage, a foothold among teachers and officials, and the king's tolerance.

5.name: Jhāpāli Kāmred
5.text:
In the eastern Terai district of Jhapa, across the border from Naxalbari in India, young communists such as Radha Krishna Mainali, Chandra Prakash Mainali and Mohan Chandra Adhikari have turned away from the quarrelling party leaderships. Inspired by the Naxalbari peasant uprising of 1967 and Charu Majumdar, they are building secret cells among landless peasants and students.

They reject both the Panchayat and parliamentary politics and preach the annihilation of class enemies: armed attacks on landlords and moneylenders to ignite a peasant revolution on Mao's path. They are hostile to Moscow, to India's government and to the palace. Their leverage lies in the misery of Jhapa's tenants and their readiness for violence.

6.name: Kodāri-pakshya
6.text:
Since the Chinese-built road from Kathmandu to the Tibetan border at Kodari opened in 1967, a nationalist camp in the palace, the bureaucracy and the press has looked north for a counterweight to India. It backed the government's demand of June 1969 that the Indian military liaison group and the Indian wireless posts on the northern frontier be withdrawn.

These hardline royalists see India as the main threat to Nepal's sovereignty and Indian-backed Congress democrats as a fifth column, and they value Chinese aid, Pakistani friendship and Soviet goodwill as balance. They oppose Western missionaries and liberal reform alike. Their leverage lies in the king's own drive for independence from Delhi.

7.name: Gāun Pharka Rāshtriya Abhiyān
7.english: Back to the Village National Campaign
7.text:
Launched by King Mahendra in 1967, the Back to the Village National Campaign sends officials, students and Panchayat activists into the countryside to spread the partyless philosophy and supervise local development. Directed from the palace, it is being groomed as the watchdog of Panchayat orthodoxy and a channel for reporting dissent.

Its creed is that party politics is a foreign import that divides the nation and that only the king and the class organisations can unite it. It treats Congress and communist activists, Indian influence and Western liberal ideas with equal suspicion. Its leverage lies in palace backing, a network of zonal committees and its growing power over local careers.

8.name: Imāmbāra Committee
8.text:
Nepal's Muslims, about three percent of the population, live mostly in the Terai, and in the western border towns near Lucknow small Shia communities keep imambaras where Muharram is mourned each year. Their elders and preachers look to Lucknow, where Maulana Ghulam Askari founded the Tanzeem-ul-Makatib in 1968 to spread Shia religious schooling.

They ask the Hindu kingdom for respect for Muharram processions, land for mosques and graveyards and religious instruction for their children, and they cultivate local Panchayat leaders. Loyal to the king and wary of the communal clashes in India, they shun politics beyond their community. Their leverage is small but rests on respected families and trade.

9.name: Najaf ke Shāgird
9.text:
A handful of young Shia from the Terai and from Lucknow study in the seminaries of Najaf, where Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has taught in exile since 1965. They bring home a sharper, political Shiism that the quiet imambara elders of Nepal find unsettling.

They argue that Muslims must live under Islamic law guided by the jurists, that a Hindu kingdom can never be their true home, and that the faithful must stand against Zionism, Western imperialism and the Shah. They have no organisation in Nepal and only a few listeners among Shia youth. Their leverage is purely ideological: the prestige of Najaf and of religious learning.

10.name: Rājguru Mandali
10.text:
The Hindu religious establishment of the kingdom gathers around the Rajguru, the royal preceptor who performs the king's rites, the Bhatta priests of Pashupatinath and the administrators of the Guthi Sansthan, which since 1964 has managed the vast temple endowments. Nepal is constitutionally the world's only Hindu kingdom, and its king is venerated as an incarnation of Vishnu.

The circle defends the Hindu character of the state, the ban on conversion, cow protection, caste propriety and the sacred status of the monarchy. It opposes secularism, missionaries and leftist agitation and expects the crown to protect the dharma. Its leverage lies in religious legitimacy, temple lands and its intimacy with the palace.

11.name: Khilāfat Halqa
11.text:
A small circle of young Terai Muslims, angered by communal riots in India such as those in Ahmedabad in September 1969, by the Arab defeat of 1967 and by the burning of al-Aqsa Mosque that August, listens to preachers who blame the humiliation of Muslims on the loss of the caliphate. They meet in the madrasas and tea shops of the border towns.

They dream of a revived Khilafat uniting all Muslims, reject both Hindu monarchy and secular nationalism, and speak of jihad to defend the community. They have no leader, no weapons and few followers, and the police watch them closely. Their only leverage is the anger of a poor and marginal minority.

12.name: Tarāi Islāmi Halqa
12.text:
Educated Muslims in Terai towns such as Nepalgunj, Birgunj and Biratnagar have formed study circles inspired by Abul A'la Maududi and the Jamaat-e-Islami Hind across the border. Teachers, traders and madrasa graduates read Islamist literature in Urdu, run evening classes and seek to reform the community's religious and social life.

They want Islamic education, recognition of Muslim personal law and of Urdu, and equal citizenship in the Hindu kingdom, building an Islamic way of life from below rather than seeking power. Wary of Indian Hindu nationalism and of communism, they keep a low profile under the Panchayat. Their leverage lies in schools, mosques and links to Indian Muslim organisations.

13.name: Rāshtriya Panchāyat
13.text:
The Rastriya Panchayat is the partyless national assembly created by King Mahendra's constitution of 1962, chosen indirectly through a pyramid of village, district and zonal panchayats and the official class organisations. The king appoints the council of ministers; since April 1969 it has been headed by Kirti Nidhi Bista, whose government has asked India to withdraw its military liaison group from Kathmandu.

The Panchas hold that partyless democracy suits Nepal's traditions, that development must be guided from above and that non-alignment between India and China safeguards independence. They suppress parties as divisive. Their leverage lies in royal favour, local patronage and control of development budgets.

14.name: Nepāl Kisān Sangathan
14.text:
The Nepal Peasants' Organisation is the largest of the class organisations recognised by the 1962 constitution and elects its own members to the Rastriya Panchayat. In practice it is led by village headmen, Brahmin and Chhetri landholders and Terai zamindars who sit atop the village panchayats.

It speaks for a conservative agrarian order: credit, irrigation and fertiliser for farmers, gradual implementation of the 1964 land reform, tenant rights only where they do not threaten landholders, and loyalty to the king and the Hindu order. It keeps away from both blocs and from party politics. Its leverage lies in the millions of rural households it claims to represent.

15.name: Mārwāri Seth
15.text:
Marwari merchant families, originally from Rajasthan, dominate Nepal's modern trade and industry: jute and sugar mills, the rice and textile trade and the import business along the Indian border. Houses such as the Golchhas of Biratnagar, together with Rana investors, own most of the private industry built since the Biratnagar Jute Mills opened in 1936.

They want stable rule, open trade with India, low taxes and protected licences, and they fund the Panchas who grant them. Seen as Indian outsiders by nationalists and as exploiters by the left, they avoid open politics. Their leverage lies in their capital, their credit networks and their control of essential imports.

16.name: Lhāsā Newār
16.text:
For centuries Newar merchants of Kathmandu kept trading houses in Lhasa, carrying Indian goods across the Himalaya. Since the Chinese takeover of Tibet and the tightening of the border after 1959, many have come home to the bazaars of Asan, Indra Chowk and Patan, joined by Thakali traders of the Kali Gandaki who have lost their salt trade.

They want free movement of goods across both the Indian and Tibetan borders, low duties, fewer state monopolies and an end to licence favouritism for Marwari importers. Their liberalism is that of the shopkeeper and caravan trader. Their leverage lies in Kathmandu's commerce, credit and guild networks, and in the city's old Newar elites.

17.name: Gaidā Gasti
17.text:
The armed Gaida Gasti was formed in the 1960s to stop poachers slaughtering the great one-horned rhinoceros of Chitwan, whose numbers collapsed after the valley was opened to settlers and malaria was eradicated. Around it gather forest officers, royal hunters turned naturalists and foreign advisers urging a national park in Chitwan.

They want protected areas, an end to forest clearance for resettlement, controlled timber cutting and protection of the tiger and rhino, which they present as national treasures. They depend on royal favour, since Chitwan is a royal hunting ground, and on foreign conservation bodies. Their leverage lies in the palace's pride and in international attention.

18.name: Nepāl Prajā Parishad
18.text:
Founded in 1936 as the first underground movement against Rana rule, the Nepal Praja Parishad gave the country its martyrs of 1941 and, in Tanka Prasad Acharya, the prime minister of 1956–57 who opened relations with China. Banned with all parties since 1961, it survives as a circle of veterans and followers around Acharya.

It stands for socialist planning, land reform, a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament and strict non-alignment, with a marked suspicion of Indian domination and sympathy for Peking. It cooperates with the left against the Panchayat when it can. Its leverage lies in its moral standing as the pioneer of the democratic struggle.

19.name: Nepāl Kamyunist Pārti (Pushpa Lāl)
19.text:
Pushpa Lal Shrestha, who founded the Communist Party of Nepal in 1949 and translated the Communist Manifesto into Nepali, broke with the compromisers of the Rayamajhi leadership and in 1968 reorganised his followers as a separate party. He operates from exile in India, with cells in the Kathmandu valley and the Terai.

He holds that the Panchayat autocracy is the main enemy and calls for a united front with the Nepali Congress to restore parliamentary democracy as a step toward people's democracy. Sympathetic to China yet independent of both Moscow and Peking, the party rejects terrorism and ultra-left adventures. Its leverage lies in Pushpa Lal's prestige and a loyal student following.

20.name: Nepāl Bhutpurva Sainik Sangathan
20.text:
Tens of thousands of Nepalis have served in the British and Indian Gurkha regiments and returned to the hills of Gorkha, Gulmi, Lamjung and the east as lahure, pensioners with savings and prestige. The Nepal Ex-Servicemen's Organisation, one of the class organisations of the Panchayat system, channels their voice in the Rastriya Panchayat.

Its politics are a soldierly populism: loyalty to the king, pride in the Gorkha martial tradition, demands for pensions, land, schools and roads in the hill districts, and contempt for Kathmandu's bureaucrats and party politicians alike. Its leverage lies in the respect veterans command in their villages and their ability to mobilise them.

21.name: Hindu Adhirājya Rakshak
21.text:
A militant fringe of Hindu nationalists in Brahmin and Chhetri families, the officer corps and the Terai towns, drawn to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh across the border, wants the Hindu kingdom to be a fortress. They regard the king as protector of a Hindu-Gorkha nation besieged by communists, Christian missionaries, Muslims and Indian secularism.

They call for a disciplined national order under the crown, a permanent ban on parties, harsh punishment of proselytising and cow slaughter, and a militarised youth trained in Gorkha values. They despise both blocs. They have no legal organisation, but their leverage lies in sympathetic officers, priests and Panchayat hardliners.

22.name: Shāhi Nepāli Senā
22.text:
The Royal Nepal Army, descended from the Gorkha army that unified the country under Prithvi Narayan Shah, is a small infantry force answerable to the king as supreme commander rather than to any minister. Its officers come overwhelmingly from Chhetri and Thakuri families tied to the court and the Ranas, and it carried out the arrest of the elected government in December 1960.

The army sees itself as the sword of the dynasty and the guardian against Congress insurgents and communist agitation, and it receives training and equipment from India, Britain and the United States. It stays out of daily politics. Its leverage lies in being the ultimate guarantee of royal power.

23.name: Shāh Vamsha
23.text:
King Mahendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev, on the throne since 1955, dismissed the elected Nepali Congress government in December 1960, banned all parties and in 1962 imposed the partyless Panchayat system under a constitution that vests sovereignty in the crown. Heir to the Gorkha kings who unified Nepal in the eighteenth century, he rules as head of state and Hindu sovereign; Crown Prince Birendra is to marry Aishwarya Rana in February 1970.

Mahendra pursues guided development, land reform and a non-aligned foreign policy balancing India, China, the Soviet Union and the West. The crown's leverage is near total: the army, the palace secretariat and the appointment of every minister.
